brief.head: Empire on a tenth
brief.text: The UK of 1910 ruled the world on about 10 per cent of GDP, Ajay Shah said. The size of the Indian state, in his view, is way over­done. {121-C03}

brief.head: Square the rate
brief.text: Economic dis­tor­tion rises roughly[[x1]] with the square of the tax rate, Shah said. Going from 8 or 9 per cent to 16 or 18 mul­ti­plies it by four. {#fourx}

brief.head: Late is a tax too
brief.text: When input tax credit comes back slowly[[x2]], firms pay in­ter­est on work­ing cap­i­tal the gov­ern­ment holds. That in­ter­est, Shah said, is it­self a tax. {#late}

brief.head: Give me tariffs
brief.text: Cascading taxes make a for­eign shirt at 300 look cheap be­side an Indian one at 440, Shah said, and do­mes­tic firms then lobby for tar­iffs. {#tariffs}

brief.head: Ideas come first
brief.text: Busy civil ser­vants are mostly fire­fight­ing[[x4]], Shah said. Real progress in India hap­pens up­stream of pol­i­cy­mak­ers[[x3]]: in pa­pers, books, blogs and sem­i­nars. {121-C10}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on the tax he helped name, and how to mend it
lead.head: The tax that lost its heart

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 121

play.label: Hear the case for a fix

body: A few morn­ings ear­lier, the *Business Standard* had car­ried a col­umn by Vijay Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah on how India’s GST could be made much bet­ter. Policymakers, Amit Varma said, “squealed in de­light, un­less they were part of gov­ern­ment, where they squealed in em­bar­rass­ment”.
The same three had writ­ten the paper that first brought the GST into Indian pol­icy cir­cles. They did not like the shape it took, Varma said.

Shah’s di­ag­no­sis was stark. The GST was meant to be a value added tax, and a VAT lives by the flow of input tax credit from one stage of pro­duc­tion to the next. In India, that flow is in­creas­ingly blocked.
“If you don’t have cor­rect han­dling of input tax credit, then it’s not a VAT,” he said. “Then you’re back to pro­duc­tion tax, you’re back to cas­cad­ing taxes.” {121-C08}
## Growth first

Shah began where, he said, every ques­tion about the state should begin: eco­nomic growth. Growth comes from high-productivity firms, and they rest on three pil­lars: spe­cial­i­sa­tion, learn­ing by doing and glob­al­i­sa­tion.
“So the job of the tax sys­tem is never ever mess with these three,” he said. “Do not come in the way.” {121-C01}
A cas­cad­ing tax, charged on every sale, does ex­actly that. It taxes tax on tax, and in Shah’s worked ex­am­ple a “mild” 10 per cent on each sale of a 400-rupee shirt ended up as 25 per cent.
Among econ­o­mists, he said, “bad tax” is no mild phrase: “bad taxes are mind-blowingly stupid things that only an idiot would ever do.” {121-C04}
Such taxes pun­ish spe­cial­i­sa­tion and hob­ble ex­porters.
## Taxing the value added
The way out, Shah said, was one of the great ad­vances of 20th-century eco­nom­ics: the value added tax, in­vented by the French econ­o­mist Maurice Lauré in 1954.
Each seller deducts the tax al­ready paid up­stream. Run the same shirt through a VAT and the gov­ern­ment col­lects 40 ru­pees, a true 10 per cent, how­ever the work is split among firms.
“The travel of input tax credit is the en­gine, is the heart of the VAT,” Shah said. {121-C05}
Exports are zero-rated, so goods com­pete abroad at tax-free prices. And a good VAT has a low rate, a sin­gle rate and a com­pre­hen­sive base.
## A tax in name
India’s GST, an­nounced in 2016 and launched in 2017, broke all three of those rules: many rates, cesses, and whole sec­tors such as elec­tric­ity, pe­tro­leum and real es­tate left out.
Worse, Shah said, the block­ages keep spread­ing. Some goods taxed at 5 per cent have their credit blocked, so the real bur­den is far higher.
Varma, who had long called the GST great in con­cept and ter­ri­ble in im­ple­men­ta­tion, said he had not known how many ways the credit was being blocked.
The hosts traced the drift to who writes tax pol­icy. Power has shifted to the tax ad­min­is­tra­tors of the Department of Revenue, and in the meet­ings that block credit, no­body asks about GDP.

The fix, Shah said, is the orig­i­nal pre­scrip­tion, be­gin­ning with the re­moval of every block­age. “So the an­swer is ex­actly where we were in 2003,” he said. “Have a sin­gle rate, have a low rate, with a com­pre­hen­sive base, and I’m em­bar­rassed to say with no block­ages against input tax credit.” {121-C11}
“It is a long game, it is a hard fight,” Varma said.

second.label: Origin story
second.head: A VAT by any other name
second.deck: Why Ajay Shah and his co-authors coined ‘goods and services tax’ in 2003

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on why it is not called VAT

body: In 2003, Vijay Kelkar led a com­mit­tee, ap­pointed by Jaswant Singh, on im­ple­ment­ing the FRBM Act. Working on it, Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah con­cluded that India’s fis­cal prob­lem had no way out with­out a proper VAT. {121-S02}
There was a snag. The word was taken. A cen­tral VAT, CENVAT, was start­ing to hap­pen, but it was not a VAT: it did not han­dle input tax credit or ser­vices cor­rectly.
So they coined a new name, Shah said, to avoid ex­plain­ing “the twenty ways in which that was not quite a VAT”. The name ap­peared in a com­mit­tee re­port in 2003. {#report}

quote.text: So we coined the phrase goods and ser­vices tax as a way to just dis­tin­guish to make sure there’s no con­fu­sion

third.head: Tax-free on the high seas

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on zero-rating of exports

body: When an Indian shirt is sold to a for­eigner, Ajay Shah said, a good VAT charges no tax at all. The ex­porter also claims back the input tax credit built up along the way. {121-C06}
“You do not tax for­eign­ers. Don’t bring na­tion­al­ism into this,” he said, brush­ing aside talk of a level play­ing field. Good tax­a­tion, he said, is not pop­ulis­tic.
On the high seas, then, the shirt’s price is im­mune to tax­a­tion, and coun­tries with high and low VAT rates com­pete on equal terms.

At its des­ti­na­tion the shirt pays the local VAT. “The French are very so­cial­ist,” Shah said, “so they have a 20% VAT.” {121-J08} The im­porter pays 80 ru­pees at the bor­der, and a French shirt­maker faces the same 20 per cent.

box.title: The papers behind the episode
box.text: In a 2003 com­mit­tee re­port, Vijay Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah coined the name GST. Now, in their col­umn *To GST or not to GST*, they doc­u­ment how input tax credit has been blocked, and pre­scribe the same cure. {121-C11}

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Just grow your own Google
sections.caption: the three engines of firm productivity
body: Every ques­tion about the state, Ajay Shah said, should start with eco­nomic growth. And growth is easy: “You just have to get NVIDIA and Google emerge out of the Indian soil.” {121-J02}
High-productivity firms, he said, have three in­gre­di­ents. The first is spe­cial­i­sa­tion, Adam Smith’s pin idea: a jack of all trades is a mas­ter of none.

The sec­ond is learn­ing by doing, via Wright’s Law and cost ex­pe­ri­ence curves[[x7]]. Shah bor­rowed Amit Varma’s phrase for it: put in vol­ume. “If you’ve made 10,000 pins, you ain’t seen noth­ing yet.” {121-J11}
The third is glob­al­i­sa­tion: re­mov­ing the thicket of bar­ri­ers at the bor­der to cap­i­tal, labour, goods, ser­vices and en­ter­prise.
Varma pointed to the show’s episode on Lant Pritchett’s work: every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor de­pends on per capita GDP ris­ing, and growth is the only way out of poverty.
## A small state
The state, Shah said, needs money for peace, easy taxes, a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice[[x6]] and a few ba­sics. He would rather the Indian state taxed less and spent less. {121-C03}

Offer a pol­i­cy­maker 15 ru­pees of tax on a GDP of 100, or 15 on a GDP of 200, and too many in Indian tax­a­tion see no dif­fer­ence. Shah would take the big­ger GDP: tax pol­icy ex­ists to serve the peo­ple. {121-C02}
~ The tax system’s one duty, Shah said, is to stay out of the way of the three en­gines of firm pro­duc­tiv­ity.

quote.text: In about 10% of GDP, you can be­come the UK of 1910.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the three engines of firm productivity

sections.label: The bad tax
sections.head: The monster in the invoice
sections.caption: the cascading tax on production
body: Among econ­o­mists, Ajay Shah said, “bad tax” is not a mild phrase. A hand­ful of taxes are good, and every other scheme known to man is bad.
One ex­am­ple is the cas­cad­ing tax, levied at every stage of pro­duc­tion. A 10 per cent tax on each sale of a shirt, from cot­ton to cus­tomer, adds up to 25 per cent. {121-S01}

It strikes at two of the three pil­lars of growth. Firms stop spe­cial­is­ing, be­cause one com­pany that runs from petro­chem­i­cals to cloth es­capes the tax on each sale. “And I have a sug­gested brand name for that cloth,” Shah said. “It’s called Vimal.” {121-J04}
## Bad for trade

Exporters suf­fer too. How, Shah asked, can an Indian shirt­maker com­pete with “a coun­try with bril­liant Bengali econ­o­mists who have con­structed a su­pe­rior tax sys­tem? It’s called Bangladesh.” {121-J06}
And im­ports look cheap, so do­mes­tic firms ask for tar­iffs: “an­other night­mare”.
Shah thought every God-fearing econ­o­mist should stand up and stage a dharna. Amit Varma de­murred: “Our econ­o­mists don’t fear God. They fear gov­ern­ment.” {121-J05}
~ Varma, for his part, felt like start­ing a hash­tag: not all taxes. {121-J03}

quote.text: It sounds like a nice meek five per­cent tax, but it’s ac­tu­ally some­thing truly ter­ri­ble.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the cascading tax on production

sections.label: The French answer
sections.head: Credit where it’s due
sections.caption: the value added tax and input tax credit
body: One of the great ad­vances of 20th-century eco­nom­ics, Ajay Shah said, was the value added tax, in­vented by the French econ­o­mist Maurice Lauré in 1954. Anyone who thinks eco­nom­ics is “the bor­ing game of sit­ting in an of­fice and writ­ing R pro­grams” should think again. {121-J10}
The idea is to tax not pro­duc­tion but the value added at each stage. Every seller charges tax on its in­voice, but deducts the tax al­ready paid up­stream, which reaches it as input tax credit.

Run the 400-rupee shirt through this and each stage re­mits just 10 ru­pees: 40 in all, a true 10 per cent. One firm or four, the tax is the same. “The gov­ern­ment has no view,” Shah said, on how spe­cialised firms should be.
## The ex­port trick
Exports are zero-rated. The ex­porter charges no VAT and claims a re­fund of all its ac­cu­mu­lated credit, so ex­porters ev­ery­where com­pete on tax-free prices. {121-C06}
Without the travel of credit, Shah warned, it is not a VAT at all, just a pro­duc­tion tax “with all those dele­te­ri­ous out­comes”. {121-C05}
~ Amit Varma called it “such a beau­ti­ful, el­e­gant de­sign”.

quote.text: this sim­ple idea is trans­for­ma­tive be­cause it be­comes neu­tral to the com­plex­ity of the pro­duc­tion process.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the value added tax and input tax credit

sections.label: Getting it right
sections.head: Paratha at 18, roti at 5
sections.caption: a low, single rate on a broad base
body: A VAT done right, Ajay Shah said, rests on three prin­ci­ples. The first is a low rate. “Don’t have a value added tax of 28 per cent. That is just nuts.” {#nuts}

His pre­ferred rate for India is 8 per cent, at most 9. High rates push peo­ple to evade and back into cash[[x8]]. Distortion, he said, rises roughly with the square of the tax rate, so dou­bling the rate quadru­ples the dam­age. {121-C07}
The sec­ond is a com­pre­hen­sive base with no ex­emp­tions. Shrink the base, and “the ever thirsty gov­ern­ment” wants a higher rate. The path to a low rate lies in a broad base.
## Classification wars
The third is a sin­gle rate. Many rates, Shah said, in­vite jock­ey­ing, lob­by­ing and cor­rup­tion, and clas­si­fi­ca­tion dis­putes: India has taxed parathas at 18 per cent and rotis at 5.
Amit Varma had the clas­sic case: “is KitKat a choco­late or a bis­cuit?” {121-J12}
Multiple rates also strain a state of low ca­pa­bil­ity, Shah said. Administering one low rate on ev­ery­thing is some­thing India can man­age.
~ His ad­vice: “keep your life sim­ple”.

quote.text: The dis­tor­tion im­posed upon an econ­omy goes up roughly in pro­por­tion to the tax rate squared.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on a low, single rate on a broad base

sections.label: The Indian journey
sections.head: From excise to a leaky GST
sections.caption: the blocking of input tax credit
body: India began with ex­cise, a tax on pro­duc­tion col­lected by an in­spec­tor at the fac­tory gate, Ajay Shah said. {#excise} Later came a cas­cad­ing tax on ser­vices.

In 2004 Chidambaram, as fi­nance min­is­ter, chose not to pur­sue the GST, cit­ing a lack of sup­port in state gov­ern­ments. The BJP re­fused to take part in tax re­form. Yet the au­thors had pro­posed a route around the states: the Centre could build the tax for it­self and let states join later. {121-S03}
Arun Jaitley, as fi­nance min­is­ter, re­vived it: the GST was an­nounced in 2016 and launched in 2017. {#jaitley} It broke all three prin­ci­ples: many rates and cesses, whole sec­tors left out.
## Credit blocked

The gravest fail­ure[[x9]], Shah said, is the block­ing of input tax credit. Final-stage goods pro­duc­ers do not get proper credit for ser­vices and cap­i­tal goods, and ser­vices firms face blocks too. Several goods at 5 per cent have their credit blocked: “the tax­man giveth and the tax­man taketh away.” {121-J07}

Amit Varma re­called call­ing the GST “con­cep­tu­ally great, but the im­ple­men­ta­tion was ter­ri­ble”. His guest Devangshu Datta had pre­dicted the fail­ures be­fore the tax was even an­nounced. {121-S04}
~ The cure, Shah said, is to “run, not walk” and re­store seam­less end-to-end credit.

quote.text: So all the three prin­ci­ples of a good VAT were vi­o­lated in the GST as it un­folded, as it came out the front door.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the blocking of input tax credit

quote.text: The way we’ve al­ways talked about it is that the most im­por­tant change that hap­pens in the coun­try is up­stream of pol­i­cy­mak­ers. It is in the ideas, it is in the knowl­edge.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A taxed shirt, a stalled reform and a prediction that came true

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah follows one shirt from cotton to customer
stories.head: Ten per cent, four times over
body: A farmer sells cot­ton to a spin­ner for 100 ru­pees, Ajay Shah began. With a 10 per cent tax on every sale, 10 ru­pees go to the gov­ern­ment.
The spin­ner sells yarn to a weaver for 200: an­other 20 ru­pees in tax. The fab­ric goes to a tai­lor for 300: 30 more. The tai­lor sells the shirt to a cus­tomer for 400: 40 more.
The cus­tomer pays 440 and may think 10 per cent is not so bad. But, as Amit Varma tot­ted up, 100 ru­pees have gone to the gov­ern­ment.
Once you see the whole chain, Shah said, you can’t unsee it. “On a 400 rupee shirt, the gov­ern­ment got 100 ru­pees of tax,” he said. “That’s 25%.” {121-S01}
~ Then he ran the same shirt through a VAT. Each seller deducts the tax al­ready paid up­stream, so each stage sends only 10 ru­pees to the gov­ern­ment. The total is 40: a true 10 per cent. {#forty}
stories.why: The same 10 per cent can mean 25 or 10 de­pend­ing on de­sign alone. What mat­ters is not the head­line rate but whether tax is piled on tax, which is why Shah counts the cas­cad­ing tax among the bad taxes. {121-C04}

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the road from a 2003 report to the GST
stories.head: A decade in the pending tray
body: Ajay Shah and his co-authors had pro­posed the GST in a 2003 com­mit­tee re­port. They also of­fered a route that did not need every state on board: the Centre could build an in­te­grated tax on goods and ser­vices for it­self, and states could join later. {121-S03}

In 2004, Chidambaram, as fi­nance min­is­ter, chose not to pur­sue it. Partly, Shah said, he cited a lack of sup­port from state gov­ern­ments. The BJP said it would not take part in any tax pol­icy re­form.
“So the things were kicked for­ward till 2014,” Shah said. The Congress was in power for ten years. {#kicked}
Then Arun Jaitley, as fi­nance min­is­ter, got back to the project. The GST was an­nounced in 2016, launched in 2017 and has been amended many times since.
~ By then its rates were, in Shah’s words, “as­tro­nom­i­cally high”, and elec­tric­ity, pe­tro­leum and real es­tate were left out.
stories.why: A good idea can be adopted in name and lose its core on the way. By the time the GST came out of the front door, Shah said, all three prin­ci­ples of a good VAT had been vi­o­lated.
stories.postscript: Today, Shah said, the an­swer is ex­actly where it was in 2003. {121-C11}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the road from 2003 to 2017

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on demonetisation, the GST and an early warning
stories.head: Devangshu Datta saw it coming
body: In the early days of *The Seen and the Unseen*, Amit Varma said, episodes were not long deep dives. Each looked at one pol­icy, and he did early episodes on de­mon­eti­sa­tion and many on the GST.

He judged the two very dif­fer­ently. “Demonetisation was just a dis­as­trous pol­icy mea­sure, con­cep­tu­ally wrong, ev­ery­thing was bad about it,” he said. “But GST was con­cep­tu­ally great, but the im­ple­men­ta­tion was ter­ri­ble.” {121-S04}

His first GST guest was their friend Devangshu Datta, who cor­rectly pre­dicted ev­ery­thing that would go wrong, be­fore the GST was even an­nounced. A later episode with Shruti Rajagopalan was com­pre­hen­sive.

~ Now, Varma said, Ajay Shah’s ac­count of blocked input tax credit wor­ried him deeply. Credit has to work prop­erly, he said, or what is the point? He had not known it was blocked in so many ways. {#aware}
stories.why: Separate a policy’s con­cept from its ex­e­cu­tion. In Varma’s view, de­mon­eti­sa­tion was wrong on both counts and the GST only on the sec­ond, and an in­formed ob­server saw the fail­ures com­ing.

quiz.q: Under a 10 per cent tax on every sale, how much tax does a 400-rupee shirt carry?
quiz.a: 100 ru­pees, an ef­fec­tive 25 per cent, in Ajay Shah’s cas­cad­ing ex­am­ple.

quiz.q: Who invented the value added tax, and in which year, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Maurice Lauré, a French econ­o­mist, in 1954, as Shah told it.

quiz.q: Why did Shah and his co-authors call it the Goods and Services Tax rather than a VAT?
quiz.a: The name VAT was taken by CENVAT, which was not re­ally a VAT.

quiz.q: What single GST rate would Ajay Shah prefer for India, and what ceiling?
quiz.a: Eight per cent, he said, and nine per cent at the very most.

quiz.q: Which classification puzzle did Amit Varma offer as the classic example of multiple GST rates?
quiz.a: Whether KitKat is a choco­late or a bis­cuit, since the two are taxed dif­fer­ently.

quiz.q: What does Shah call the heart of the VAT, which India has increasingly blocked?
quiz.a: The travel of input tax credit from one stage of pro­duc­tion to the next.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 121. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Arun Jaitley (Ministry of Defence, GODL-India); P. Chidambaram (World Economic Forum, CC BY-SA 2.0); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India).

laughs.text: Ajay on the ‘easy’ recipe for growth: ‘You just have to get NVIDIA and Google emerge out of the Indian soil.’ After list­ing the three pil­lars, he adds: ‘It’s very easy, yeah. You should try it one of these days.’
Ajay: ‘Every God fear­ing econ­o­mist should stand up and put up a dharna.’ Amit: ‘Our econ­o­mists don’t fear God. They fear gov­ern­ment. Government fear­ing econ­o­mists should be the new term.’

Ajay’s run­ning gag about the neigh­bour that got its tax sys­tem right: ‘a coun­try with bril­liant Bengali econ­o­mists who have con­structed a su­pe­rior tax sys­tem? It’s called Bangladesh... Because Bangladesh has only Bengali econ­o­mists.’
The GST clas­si­fi­ca­tion dis­putes: Amit’s ‘is KitKat a choco­late or a bis­cuit?’ and Ajay’s paratha taxed at 18% ver­sus roti at 5%, as ex­am­ples of the mess mul­ti­ple rates cre­ate.
